content.text: By the end of this lesson I can
calculate unit and non-unit proper fractions of amounts.
calculate improper fractions and mixed-number fractions of amounts.
In 3/8, which number is the numerator?

slides.notes:
Answers: 1. 24 ÷ 6 = 4. Sharing 24 into 6 equal groups gives 4 in each group. 2. 7 × 4 = 28. Four groups of 7 make 28. 3. The numerator is 3 and the denominator is 8. The numerator is the top number; the denominator is the bottom number. If an answer to question 1 is not 4, revisit division facts. If an answer to question 2 is not 28, revisit the 7 times table. If the numbers in question 3 are swapped, recap the names of the top and bottom numbers in a fraction.
Answers: 1. 4 2. 28 3. 3

content.text: The denominator sets the equal parts
There are 24 cakes. One quarter of the tray holds 6 cakes.
The denominator is the bottom number. It tells us how many equal parts make one whole.
A unit fraction has 1 on top. Divide the amount by the denominator.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: A tray of 24 cakes is split into four equal parts of 6 cakes, with one part shaded.

slides.notes: Our bakery tray holds 24 cakes. Eventually we must work out an order of 1 5/6 trays. Start with one quarter of a tray. Point to the four equal parts: 24 ÷ 4 = 6. The denominator counts the equal parts, not the cakes in each part. Explain that the whole here is one full tray.

content.text: How many cakes are in 3/4 of a tray of 24 cakes?

slides.notes: A proper fraction has a numerator smaller than its denominator. The numerator is the top number: it counts the parts we need. A non-unit fraction has more than 1 on top. Show the first line, then ask the class for each later line before revealing it. Three quarters means three of the equal parts, so 6 × 3 = 18. State the general method: divide by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator. This also works for unit fractions, where the numerator is 1.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: A tray of 24 cakes is split into four equal parts of 6 cakes, with one part shaded.

slides.notes:
Answers: 30 ÷ 5 = 6 cakes; 30 ÷ 3 = 10 and 10 × 2 = 20 cakes. Ask pupils to propose the first calculation, then complete the working together. Multiplying by the denominator suggests that equal sharing is not secure. Dividing by the numerator suggests that the two fraction numbers have been confused. Return to the equal parts of the tray if needed.
Answers: 1. 6 cakes 2. 20 cakes

content.text: Improper fractions can exceed one whole
Each quarter-tray holds 6 cakes. Five quarters hold 30 cakes.
An improper fraction has a numerator at least as large as its denominator.
Four quarters make one tray. Five quarters need one extra quarter-tray.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: One complete tray has four shaded parts of 6 cakes, and a second tray has one shaded part of 6 cakes.

slides.notes: Count the five shaded quarter-trays. Each has the same size: 24 ÷ 4 = 6. Altogether, 6 × 5 = 30. A fraction is not always less than one whole. If the numerator equals the denominator, it is exactly one whole; if it is larger, the fraction is greater than one. The unshaded spaces are not part of the order.

content.text: How many cakes are in 7/6 of a tray of 24 cakes?

slides.notes: Show the first line. Ask the class for each later line before revealing it. The method has not changed: divide by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator. Here 24 ÷ 6 = 4 and 4 × 7 = 28. Six sixths fill a tray; the seventh sixth adds 4 cakes. This explains why 28 cakes is a sensible answer.

content.text: How many cakes are in 1 2/3 trays if one tray holds 24 cakes?

slides.notes: A mixed number has a whole-number part and a fraction part. Show the first line, then ask for each later line before revealing it. One whole contains three thirds, so 1 2/3 = 5/3. Then use the same method: 24 ÷ 3 = 8 and 8 × 5 = 40. To convert any mixed number, count the denominator's number of parts for each whole, then include the numerator's extra parts. Keep the same denominator.

content.text: What is 5/4 of a batch of 16 cakes?

slides.notes: The answer is 20: 16 ÷ 4 = 4 and 4 × 5 = 20. The answer 12 can come from treating five quarters as three quarters to keep the result below a whole: 4 × 3 = 12. This reveals the main misconception. The answer 4 stops after finding one quarter: 16 ÷ 4 = 4. The answer 80 ignores the denominator: 16 × 5 = 80. If pupils choose a wrong answer, revisit the five shaded quarter-parts before independent practice.

content.text: Your turn: find fractions of cake orders
1: Find 1/3 of 18 cakes and explain why you divide by 3 first.
2: Find 3/5 of 35 cakes and explain why you multiply by 3 next.
3: Explain why 9/8 of 32 cakes is greater than 32, using the numerator.
4: A tray holds 24 cakes; find how many cakes are needed for 1 5/6 trays and explain your method.

slides.notes: Work alone. Item 1: 18 ÷ 3 = 6 cakes. Item 2: 35 ÷ 5 = 7 and 7 × 3 = 21 cakes. Item 3: 32 ÷ 8 = 4 and 4 × 9 = 36 cakes. A good explanation says that the numerator counts nine eighths, whereas eight eighths already make the whole batch; the extra eighth adds 4 cakes. Item 4 settles the opening bakery order: 1 = 6/6, so 1 5/6 = 11/6; 24 ÷ 6 = 4 and 4 × 11 = 44 cakes. Harder challenge: an order of 2 3/4 trays contains 66 cakes; how many cakes fit one tray? Answer: 2 3/4 = 11/4, 66 ÷ 11 = 6 cakes per quarter-tray, and 6 × 4 = 24 cakes per tray.

misconceptions.belief: A fraction of an amount must be smaller than the amount. In fact, a fraction greater than one gives more than the original amount: the denominator sets the equal parts and the numerator counts them.
